title: Delhi High Court Orders Fresh Notice in Amrit Wilson OCI Cancellation Case
excerpt: Justice Amit Mahajan held that the 2023 order cancelling the UK-based author's OCI card named no specific 'anti-India activities,' denying her a chance to respond — and set a fixed timetable for the Centre to redo the process.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has held that the Centre's 2023 order cancelling UK-based author Amrit Wilson's OCI card named no specific "anti-India activities," so she had no real opportunity to answer the allegations.
  • Justice Amit Mahajan directed the authorities to issue a fresh show cause notice within one week, spelling out the specific reasons — or, where material is sensitive, a redacted gist of it.
  • Wilson must reply within one week of the fresh notice, and the authorities must pass a fresh order within two weeks after that; the existing cancellation stays operative for up to four weeks in the meantime.
  • For OCI cardholders generally: the ruling confirms a cancellation notice must state the case the holder has to meet — a bare allegation of "anti-India activities" is not enough.

The Delhi High Court has found that the order cancelling the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card of UK-based author and journalist Amrit Wilson did not specify the alleged anti-India activities attributed to her, and has directed the Centre to start the process again — this time with the allegations spelled out. Justice Amit Mahajan held that the principles of natural justice were not followed, because neither the show cause notice nor the cancellation order disclosed specific details of what Wilson was said to have done, according to LiveLaw's report of the ruling.

Who Wilson is, and what was cancelled

Wilson was born in India and lived there until 1961, when she moved to the United Kingdom for higher studies. She settled in the UK and worked as a writer, journalist and social activist. She surrendered her Indian passport and acquired a British passport in 2009, was issued a Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card in 2014, and was granted an OCI card on December 20, 2017. The OCI status is what allowed her to live and work in India indefinitely; its cancellation in 2023 effectively barred her from entering the country.

How the cancellation unfolded

In November 2022, the authorities issued Wilson a show cause notice alleging that she was engaged in "detrimental propaganda against the Indian government" and had been involved in multiple anti-India activities said to be inimical to India's sovereignty and integrity, security and public interest. The notice gave her 15 days to explain why her OCI card should not be cancelled under Section 7D(e) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 — the provision that lets the government cancel an OCI registration on grounds including activity prejudicial to India's sovereignty, security or public interest.

Wilson replied denying any involvement in anti-India activities. She pointed out that the notice disclosed no specific allegations against her, and asked for the material behind it so she could present her case. The authorities sent no further communication for three months, and then cancelled her OCI registration on March 17, 2023. She challenged that order in the Delhi High Court.

"A perusal of the SCN and the impugned order indicates that the same is bereft of any specific details of Anti-India activities in which the petitioner was involved, thus, providing no opportunity to the petitioner to provide an explanation in respect of the same."

— Delhi High Court, in the Amrit Wilson OCI case

What the court held

Before the court, Wilson's counsel argued that the authorities had never disclosed the specific incidents behind the cancellation — and that even in their counter-affidavit, the respondents had not given reasons, saying the material could only be placed before the court in a sealed cover. Justice Mahajan noted that neither the notice nor the order contained specific details, and that no specific reasons had been provided in the counter-affidavit either. "It is trite law that a SCN must specifically indicate the case that a noticee has to meet," the court said. It added that Wilson's rights under Section 7B of the Citizenship Act — the section that carries the rights and privileges of an OCI cardholder — could not be taken away without giving her an appropriate opportunity to respond.

The other side of the record

The Centre's position throughout has been that the material against Wilson includes intelligence inputs that cannot be fully disclosed. At an earlier hearing in the same case, a different bench examined a sealed-cover report from the government and remarked that the allegations went beyond a couple of social media posts, observing that the country cannot be allowed to be maligned on international platforms, Bar and Bench reported. Wilson's counsel at that hearing argued that none of her work was anti-India, and that posts on the farmers' protest and Kashmir that the government had referred to publicly were not the stated basis of the notice. The new ruling does not decide whether Wilson engaged in any anti-India activity; it decides only that she must be told, specifically, what she is accused of before her status can be taken away.

What happens next

The timetable is now fixed. The authorities must issue a fresh show cause notice within one week, setting out the specific reasons for cancellation. If the reasons cannot be disclosed in full, Wilson must be given the gist of the material with sensitive information redacted, or be allowed to inspect the material that led to the cancellation. She then has one week to reply, and the authorities must pass a fresh order within two weeks of that. Until then, the existing cancellation order remains operative for four weeks or until the fresh order is passed, whichever is earlier — so Wilson's OCI status is not restored by this ruling, and the substantive fight over the allegations is still to come.
nri_angle: For OCI cardholders, the ruling sets a procedural floor: before a cancellation can stand, the government must spell out the specific allegations — or at least a redacted gist — so the holder can actually answer them.
